title: The Wrong Choir
premise: Freya Fairweather, a pest controller who has spent seven years rationalizing the impossible sounds beneath the town of Hollowmere, is summoned when an excavation crew unearths a stone door sealed from the inside. The door belongs to the town's founders, who bound something in exchange for their prosperity, and the binding is failing because the ritual requires a choir of willing voices—voices that have been dying out for generations. As Freya investigates, she discovers her own family were the last keepers, that her invisibility was engineered by those who wanted no witnesses, and that the entity offers power to anyone who completes its half of the bargain. Refusing both the founders' cruelty and the entity's seduction, Freya assembles a choir of the town's overlooked and discarded—the people the powerful never counted—and finishes the ritual on her own terms: not to bind the thing forever, but to send it home, at the cost of her own voice and her place in the world she finally chose.
about_author: Ivo Ishikawa is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade documenting the basements of old New England towns before turning to horror. They write about the debts small communities bury and the people hired to notice what everyone else agrees not to see.

chapters.title: Something with Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Freya. Called to the Hollowmere grange hall after reports of scratching behind the walls, Freya finds greasy handprints eight feet up a plaster wall—and tells herself it's raccoons. The beat is professional denial cracking at one seam.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: POV shifts briefly to crew foreman Dale Okafor. His backhoe strikes dressed stone twelve feet below the old meetinghouse lot; the crew goes quiet when they realize the slab has no outside hinges. Beat: ordinary men deciding, together, not to look too hard.

chapters.title: Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: Freya, hired to 'deal with whatever's under there,' descends into the pit. The door's bolt mechanism only works from within. She photographs it, lies to the historical society, and takes a rubbing of carved notation she almost recognizes. Beat: curiosity overriding seven years of discipline.

chapters.title: The Fairweather File
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At home she finds her late mother's pest-control ledgers—identical handprints documented in 1989, 1961, 1933, always followed by a page torn out. Beat: the sick recognition that this was inherited, not discovered.

chapters.title: Choir Loft
chapters.summary: Historical society archivist Miriam Vance shows Freya photos of the founding congregation, all holding sheet music with the same notation from the door. Every founder died rich; every choir member's name is inked over. Beat: the first real dread.

chapters.title: The Hum
chapters.summary: Night, Freya's POV. The hum she's heard for seven years under her own floorboards resolves into distinct voices, harmonizing, waiting. She records it; playback shows forty seconds of silence. Beat: isolation—her evidence refuses to exist.

chapters.title: Dale's Last Shift
chapters.summary: Dale Okafor's POV, final night of excavation. He hears his dead brother singing a lullaby from behind the door and starts unbarring it before the crew pulls him away. He resigns at dawn, pale, and leaves town. Beat: the cost of listening.

chapters.title: Ink Over Names
chapters.summary: Freya and Miriam cross-reference the blacked-out choir names against parish death records: none of them died. They simply stop appearing anywhere after the founders' prosperity began. Beat: justice theme surfaces—prosperity bought with erased people.

chapters.title: What the Town Owes
chapters.summary: Freya confronts mayor-select Cornelius Ash, whose family founded Hollowmere. He is courteous, offers her a generous contract to declare the site structurally unsound and fill it with concrete. Beat: corruption wearing a cardigan; Freya declines and feels the town's eyes turn.

chapters.title: Vandalism
chapters.summary: Freya's van is burned; her contracts dry up overnight. Anonymous note: 'Finish your mother's work or leave.' Beat: belonging weaponized—she was never invisible, she was contained.

chapters.title: Mother's Torn Pages
chapters.summary: Searching her mother's storage unit, Freya finds the torn ledger pages hidden in a false bottom: instructions for the Rite of Return, half in the founder's notation, half in her mother's handwriting. The final verse is missing. Beat: grief braided with purpose.

chapters.title: The Undercroft
chapters.summary: Freya breaks into the sealed meetinghouse basement at night. Behind the door: a chamber shaped like an amphitheater, benches facing a central stone, and forty niches—thirty-nine holding folded clothes, one empty, sized for her. Beat: the story stops being about a place and becomes about her.

chapters.title: Voices in the Walls
chapters.summary: Miriam's POV. She begins hearing the erased choir members singing in the archive stacks—her own grandmother's alto among them. Unlike Dale, she listens to the words: not a lure but a plea. Beat: reframing the entity's voice as testimony.

chapters.title: Ash's Bargain
chapters.summary: Cornelius Ash summons Freya to his estate and reveals the truth plainly: the founders bound a hungry presence, fed it the choir, and each generation of Ashes renews the binding with smaller offerings. He wants Freya to be this century's keeper—or its offering. Beat: power's arithmetic laid bare.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Freya walks out, knowing refusal means becoming prey. That night the hum follows her to a motel; the entity speaks through the television static—not threatening, but negotiating. It offers her everything her invisibility denied her. Beat: temptation made intimate.

chapters.title: The Discarded
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She realizes the ritual needs willing voices and begins recruiting the town's overlooked: Dale (returned), Miriam, a night nurse, two teenagers who squat in the grange, an excommunicated organist. Beat: the theme of belonging turns active—a choir of the uncounted.

chapters.title: Rehearsal One
chapters.summary: In the grange hall, the ragged group attempts the notation from the rubbing. It shouldn't be readable—but it is, instantly, like remembering rather than learning. When they hit the third phrase, every light dies and something applauds. Beat: wonder curdling.

chapters.title: Ash Cracks Down
chapters.summary: Cornelius has the grange condemned, Miriam fired, the teenagers' squat raided. His POV chapter: we see his fear—he isn't cruel by nature, he's next in line if the binding fails. Beat: antagonist humanized without excused.

chapters.title: The Empty Niche
chapters.summary: Freya returns to the undercroft alone. The empty niche now holds her mother's coat. The entity, through the walls, explains gently: her mother completed three verses of the return rite before the town stopped her. Beat: inheritance as wound; Freya weeps for the first time in the book.

chapters.title: Thirty-Nine Voices
chapters.summary: Mirium channels the erased choir through automatic writing: they don't want freedom—they want to go home, and the return rite sends the entity and its taken back through the door together. But the rite demands a fortieth voice to close the door from this side. Beat: the price is named.

chapters.title: Recruiting Ash
chapters.summary: Freya does the unthinkable: asks Cornelius to join the choir. He refuses, then wavers when shown his ancestor's ledger—the first Ash signed as a choir member before upgrading himself to keeper. Beat: the corrupt confronted with their own erased origins.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Ash's men flood the undercroft and steal the rubbing and ledger pages. Freya realizes they don't need the papers—they need time, and Ash intends to hold the town hostage until she accepts the keeper's role. Beat: despair; the choir scatters.

chapters.title: Dale Stands
chapters.summary: Dale Okafor's POV. The man who fled now guards the pit with a shotgun and his brother's lullaby hummed off-key. He buys the others one night by refusing to move. Beat: cowardice redeemed into stubbornness.

chapters.title: Rehearsal in the Dark
chapters.summary: Power cut, the choir rehearses by candlelight in the grange. Without the lights, the harmonies come easier—as if darkness is the notation's native medium. The nurse, Ruth, notices the entity harmonizing with them, learning them. Beat: intimacy with the unknown deepens.

chapters.title: The Entity's Testimony
chapters.summary: Through Ruth, a medium since childhood, the entity speaks at length: it was bound here before the town existed; the founders found it starving and made a contract it never understood. It doesn't want worship. It wants the door opened from either side. Beat: moral inversion—monster as fellow prisoner.

chapters.title: Ash's Sermon
chapters.summary: Cornelius holds an emergency town meeting, framing Freya as an outsider stirring up the founders' settled debts. Half the town turns out with torches-in-spirit. Freya attends and says nothing, letting him hang himself with fear. Beat: public power revealed as performance.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Mark
chapters.summary: Waking with a brand on her wrist—the keeper's sigil—Freya understands Ash marked her remotely to force succession. If she dies a keeper, the binding renews with her soul. Beat: the trap closes; rage clarifies plan.

chapters.title: Stealing Back Time
chapters.summary: Freya, Dale, and the teens infiltrate Ash's estate during his gala and recover the ledger pages. In his study Freya finds generations of payment records: the town's prosperity itemized against names. Beat: heist energy; evidence of the crime.

chapters.title: Ruth's Choice
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. The entity offers to spare her specifically if she abandons the rite. She refuses—not bravely, she admits, but because thirty-nine voices have become hers to carry. Beat: loyalty as the book's true magic.

chapters.title: Ash Breaks
chapters.summary: Confronted with his ancestors' signatures among the erased, Cornelius collapses—not into goodness, but into terror that he was always livestock. He gives Freya the final verse page his family hid for six generations, demanding nothing. Beat: villain broken by genealogy.

chapters.title: The Missing Verse
chapters.summary: The recovered verse requires the closer to sing their own true name—a name given freely, never written. Freya realizes her mother tore the pages because she'd chosen Freya's name to be the closing word, and couldn't do it. Beat: maternal love as the last lock.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: The hum becomes audible to the whole town; dogs howl, windows resonate. Ash's remaining loyalists barricade the meetinghouse. The choir has until the new moon—three days—to finish or the binding fails entirely and the entity comes out uninvited. Beat: ticking clock engaged.

chapters.title: Day One: Gathering
chapters.summary: Freya's choir swells unexpectedly: townsfolk who heard the hum and recognized their grandparents' voices slip into the grange to help. Forty becomes sixty becomes ninety. Beat: belonging achieved at the eleventh hour, from below.

chapters.title: Day Two: Ash's Counterstroke
chapters.summary: Ash's men seize the undercroft entrance. But his own daughter joins the choir publicly, and his enforcers—one by one—put down their crowbars and start humming. Power fails not by defeat but by defection. Beat: the corrupt regime dissolving mid-siege.

chapters.title: Day Three: The Descent
chapters.summary: The full choir enters the undercroft at dusk. Freya takes the empty niche's place at the center stone. The entity stands visible for the first time: gaunt, enormous, more frightened than frightening. Beat: awe without gore; the horror genre turned inside out.

chapters.title: The Rite of Return
chapters.summary: The choir sings all four verses. The thirty-nine erased rise from the niches as light and join the harmony, going home through the opening door. The entity pauses at the threshold, looks at Freya, and—for the first time in centuries—is thanked. Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: The Closing Word
chapters.summary: The final verse demands Freya's true name. She sings it—'Fairweather,' the name her mother gave meaning weather that passes, that doesn't stay—and the door seals itself, this time from the outside, needing no sacrifice beyond a voice freely spent. Beat: climax resolved through honesty, not violence.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Days later: the hum is gone, the prosperous families' fortunes quietly unravel, and the town must reckon with what funded it. Freya can speak only in a rasp; doctors find no cause. Beat: cost honored, justice outside any courtroom beginning.

chapters.title: The New Ledger
chapters.summary: Freya, Miriam, and Ruth establish an open archive of the erased names, read aloud annually by whoever volunteers. Cornelius, diminished, attends and reads his ancestors' victims first. Beat: institutional memory as penance; belonging rebuilt on truth.

chapters.title: Weather That Passes
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Freya's POV, a year later. A new client calls about scratching in the walls of a house two towns over. Freya listens carefully, hears only raccoons, and says so—but keeps the rubbing of the notation in her glovebox, just in case. Beat: peace earned, vigilance kept; the ending rhymes with the opening.
